Just before six o'clock. Mr. Speaker, I mentioned that I should like to place on Hansard a few statistics with regard to the county of Bruce, and I do so for various reasons. The county of Bruce is well known in Canada; it is inhabited by men and women who work for a living, who are by no means wealthy people but are small wage-earners. The population of that county is approximately 51,000. The county of Bruce is more or less unique, in that within its borders there are nine large manufacturing plants. In addition, it is a splendid agricultural district; as a matter of fact, in April, 1938, it was the second largest butter producing county in Ontario.
I should like to give some figures with regard to the unemployment situation in my riding, which should be of interest because, as I have already said, we have industry, farming and fishing there. The people of Bruce donate indirectly a large amount towards the cost of relief in this country, and a little later I intend to say a few words on their behalf. According to figures obtained from the registration branch of the Department of Labour, during the month of February, 1938, the total number on relief in Bruce county was 562, including both unemployables and those employable but unemployed at the present time. Of that number eight were from agricultural districts. A further examination of that figure shows that we had forty-eight heads of families receiving aid to which the dominion contributed. I am not saying that

The Budget*-Mr. Tomlinson
we may not have more than that number unemployed, but the others are doing their utmost to earn their own living without depending upon the government.
I should like to say to the other groups in this house, including the official opposition, that instead of criticizing the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) in connection with unemployment if they were to spend more time in advising our unemployed youth, both young men and young women, to seek by means of the youth training plan to equip thmselves to obtain employment in one of the trades, we would find a distinct improvement in the unemployment situation throughout the country. There is no doubt that during the past ten years that angle has 'been neglected. Therefore I say, if the other groups in this house

and I can speak to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group also in this connection-would endeavour to have these young people take advantage of the youth training plan that has been initiated by the minister, instead of advising them that the government will look after them, my hon. friends would be doing a real service. After all, we have many young people in the rural parts of the country who are endeavouring to earn a living, pay their way and keep out of debt; yet who are called upon to donate extensively to the cost of relief in Canada. That is a fact which has caused some dissension in certain parts of the dominion.
In the past the county of Bruce endeavoured to keep within its means, and here I might address my words to some of the larger municipalities in Canada. When I say the county of Bruce has a bonded indebtedness of only $6,000, that surprises a great many municipalities which in the past disregarded their earning power when it came to spending money. I do not mean to say that we have not splendid roads in our county; we have. We also have splendid farms which, due to the hydro, are becoming better equipped with electrical appliances. We have splendid factories and a marvellous tourist country; yet we have a bonded indebtedness of only $6,000. So it rather hurts to hear in this house, day after day, destructive criticism, especially from one of these groups on my left, directed against the minister who is endeavouring to provide some means whereby these young people may be trained for the future. We know that many of these young men are not trained and that consequently there are no openings for them. There is very little use sending them out on the farms unless they are first trained. In the summer time a farmer cannot attempt to take a
young man from the city and train him during the busy season. Right now we have employment in the county of Bruce for young men who are trained in farm work. It will not be very long before the farmers will be running all over the country looking for help. The wages may not be very high, but it will be something upon which these young people may build a future. After all, the fathers and mothers of these young people and many hon. members in this house had very little in the beginning, but they started with that very little and built up estates, and the young people of to-day must realize that they will have to do the same thing.
Next I should like to say a word in regard to agriculture. I listened with amazement to the criticism of the two trade treaties, the one of 1935 and the other of 1938, offered by the official opposition. Under those treaties our farmers have benefited to a very great extent in the export of their surplus products. I was further amazed when members of other groups rose and said, "Well, we voted for it, but we are sure it will not be of much benefit." I should like to give just one instance in which the trade treaties have been of great value to our farmers. In January under the new trade treaty we exported 30,000 head of heavy cattle to the United States. Each of those cattle would average 1.400 pounds. In, 1935 there was a reduction in the tariff of one cent a pound, and a further reduction in 1939 of half a cent, meaning a total reduction of one and one-half cents a pound. On a 1.400 pound animal that means an additional $21 to the farmer, or, in other words, a total increase of $630,000 on the 30,000 head exported in January. I am amazed to think the official opposition would vote in a bloc against that trade treaty. I shall not go further into a discussion of exports of cattle, but I do know that if in the month of January 30,000 head of cattle had been shipped to the Toronto and Montreal markets, prices would not have been six or seven cents a pound but would have been two or three cents. That is what would have happened to the price of cattle had it not been for the trade treaty.
May I add that at last the farmer now has a Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) who is willing to listen to his difficulties. We realize that because of the situation in Europe, prices of farm products have fluctuated, and in order more or less to equalize his income it becomes necessary for the farmer to have some assistance by way of legislation which will tend towards developing a cooperative method of selling. Some of us who have been interested in the difficulties of the farmers

have discussed the matter this year. We have found it extremely complicated, and it has been difficult to arrive at any definite suggestion. I am pleased, however, to see that the minister is bringing in a bill whereby an advisory committee will be set up. This measure is of great importance to the farmer, because it means that at last he will have representations from the joint cooperatives throughout the dominion who will be in a position to advise the minister of their difficulties. In fact, the minister's legislation throughout is of great importance and will have far-reaching effects on agriculture. He may not have gone as far as some of us would have liked. I should like to say here and now. however, that it is better to have some legislation that at least is legal and enforcible than to have four or five acts on the statute books only to find later that they are ultra vires and of no value. Therefore I say this is a beginning towards assisting the farmer. The time is fast approaching when individual farmers must cooperate in disposing of their goods. In my opinion the time is past when an individual farmer can sell his goods on the market of his own choice.
This government has been faced with a tremendous task so far as agriculture is concerned. In 1934 a piece of legislation known as the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was placed on the statute books. In my opinion that act has done more than any other to cause the people of Canada to lose faith in farming. There was a time when a farm was considered a gilt-edged security, but that time has passed. This government was faced with that act, but so far as the eastern and central parts of Canada are concerned it is now repealed.
I hope that this government may bring back confidence to the man who has small sums of money to lend, and thereby provide our young farmers with funds with which to commence their farming operations. It is almost impossible for a young man to start out in his career. The present government has been faced with legislation such as the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and it is now endeavouring to rectify mistakes which were made before it took office. Rather than say that this government is a "do-nothing" government I would say the former Conservative government could be described in that way. Certainly it was a "do-nothing" government. Therefore, when hon. members of the opposition attempt to say that this is a "do-nothing" government, they are speaking purely and simply from political motives-and, I would say, a very low type of politics at that.

Yes, the former Conservative government was a "do-nothing" government, under the Bennett-Manion-Stevens axis.

DEDATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I remember that a few years ago an old gentleman in British Columbia told me that Ontario was in Bruce. After listening to the remarks of the last speaker (Mr. Tomlinson), I think there may be something in that assertion.
I am going to deal quite briefly with the budget. I am sure that every hon. member was deeply impressed with the closing remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). They had the ring of a true Canadian. In an eloquent and almost pathetic manner he appealed for cooperation. I should like to quote his words which appear on page 3153 of Hansard of this year, as follows:
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is it not time for us Canadians "to see ourselves as others see us," to adopt a constructive rather than a negative attitude, and to concentrate with courage and vigour on a united effort to solve our own problems and continue the work of building a greater and better country? If only we can develop more of a national esprit de corps, if only we can recreate that spirit of cooperation, mutual helpfulness and constructive enterprise possessed by those who founded this nation at confederation, we need have no fear of the future.
In order to complete the picture, I should like to place alongside this appeal the noble words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) uttered on the night of the election in October, 1935. The Prime Minister, speaking to the people of Canada on a crosscountry broadcast, said:
In the new era which dawns to-day the struggle for the rights of the people will, in the realm of economic liberty and security, be carried on as never before. Poverty and adversity, want and misery are the enemies which Liberalism will seek to banish from our land. They have lain in wait at the gate of every Canadian home during the past five years, and their menacing mien has served to destroy the souls, as well as the minds and bodies, of an ever increasing number of men, women and
children in our land. We take up at once, as our supreme task, the endeavour to end poverty in the midst of plenty; starvation and unnecessary suffering in a land of abundance; discontent and distress in a country more blessed by providence than any other on the face of the globe, and to gain for individual lives, and for the nation as a whole, that "health and peace and sweet content" which is the rightful heritage of all.
Almost four years intervened between those two speeches, the one, the noble words of the Prime Minister and the other the defeatist remarks of the Minister of Finance. We have now before us the fourth budget. The pathetic appeal of the minister makes it quite clear that Liberalism has failed in the supreme task undertaken in 1935; the so-called enemies of Liberalism are still abroad in the land. Someone, commenting on the speech of the Minister of Finance, said:
It was rot a Dunning budget. In past years Air. Dunning endeavoured to cope with conditions facing him. He made an effort ,to face prevailing conditions; in this week's budget no such effort was made.
I should like to pick out a few of the high lights in the dark and dismal picture presented by the minister, and I think I can pick out something that will be of interest to the people of this country. The minister predicted that we shall be about $60,000,000 short of meeting our obligations during the coming year, and in estimating that deficit he did not include, as he said, the whole cost of the wheat bonus which, according to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), will amount to at least another $20,000,000. Also I understand it does not include the cost of financing the program of legislation brought down by the Minister of Agriculture a short time ago. So the picture, if truly presented, would show that, instead of a deficit of $60,000,000, we shall have one of from $90,000,000 to $100,000,000.
The next high light in the picture is that there is no relief from taxation. The sugar tax remains; the sales tax of eight per cent continues to apply. As has already been pointed out, 60 per cent of our total taxation revenues comes from the pockets of the consuming public in the form of sales tax and customs and excise taxes amounting to almost $250,000,000. This is extracted from the great mass of the Canadian people in the form of indirect taxation. So there cannot be very much comfort to the people of Canada in the government's taxation proposals.
I agree with the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) that the most onerous tax burden on the Canadian people to-day is the tax on real property. It is doing more
The Budget*-Mr. Barber

to stifle industry and prevent recovery than any other form of tax. Not only business men and property owners in the cities and towns but the farmers, with diminishing returns, are almost unable to meet the ever-increasing taxes on their land and improvements. The comparison with Great Britain which the hon. member for York South gave was interesting. It showed that of all the taxes collected by taxing bodies in Canada 35-4 per cent came from real property, while in Great Britain only 18-1 per cent came from real property. Of course, the minister would naturally point out, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) has done, that the municipalities are directly responsible. That may be true, but the municipalities are confined almost entirely to that source for revenue. The fact remains that the top burden on real property to-day is the tax imposed by the municipality on the property owner for the municipality's share of relief expenditures. It may amount to 40 per cent, 30 per cent or 20 per cent, but whatever it is, it must be assessed against the real property in the municipality. It has often been pointed out, and quite properly, that fiscal and economic policies are within the jurisdiction of the federal government. Therefore, surely it is the responsibility of the federal government to care for that portion of the unemployed who are employable. Let the federal government take over this responsibility as their own, and relieve the hard pressed municipal taxpayers.
I have touched but briefly on debt and taxation. What about expenditures? I do not object to special expenditures such as those necessary to take care of relief, unemployment, youth training and pensions, but I do protest against the enormous increase in the cost of government as indicated in increased controllable expenditure. According to the statement placed before the house by the Minister of Finance, our controllable expenditure for the coming year is estimated to be $416,372,000. This is just $43,833,000 more than was spent under the same head by the Conservative government in the last year for which they were responsible-and all that increase has occurred in a period of a little more than three years! Someone may ask: "Where did this increased expenditure go?" In the first place we have increased the number of our employees by about three thousand, and it must also be borne in mind that in the last three years we have had government by commission. That is an extremely expensive form of government, particularly when we have to pay members of such commissions

living expenses of from twenty to thirty dollars a day, in addition to travelling expenses, and fees for legal gentlemen ranging as high as two hundred dollars a day. So it is not surprising that the total cost of commissions under this government has amounted to $1,453,903.
The Minister of Labour now tells us that it is his intention to set up committees, or commissions, in each of the nine provinces, and he assures us that they will be voluntary. But we received the same assurance when the national employment commission was to be set up, and yet we found that a generous government agreed to pay its members the healthy per diem allowance of thirty dollars, plus travelling expenses. We are in hopes that the government will be able at least to cut down that rate.

subtopic: DEDATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think everyone who looks mto the system of government by commission which has been carried on by the present administration will agree that it is responsible for a great deal of the increased cost of government. There are many expenses that might be classed as extravagant, some of which were referred to this afternoon by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Hyndman), He was of opinion that expenditures in the city of Ottawa for the purpose of beautifying the capital might be classed as extravagant at this time. He pointed out that at Connaught place in the centre of this city an expenditure of $1,300,000 is being incurred. I have no objection whatever to beautifying the capital, and I would not for one moment protest against the erection of a suitable memorial to those who made the supreme sacrifice for us overseas. But surely there is a limit to these expenditures, particularly when we have throughout Canada so many returned men at the present time in need of assistance. This reminds me that I received to-day a letter from the secretary of the branch of the Canadian Legion in my district complaining that on the work which is being carried on by the federal government at this time at Nicomen island no returned man can secure a job. I hope this will be rectified because I should hate to see this government follow the practice which has been adopted by the government in our province and under which every man who wants to get a job, no matter whether he is on relief or in dire distress,

The Budget-Mr. Barber
must have in his pocket a membership ticket in the local Liberal association. I hope this government will never go that far.
The hon. member for Carleton also referred to what he termed the extravagant expenditure in the construction of the supreme court building at a cost of $3,360,000. This may be compared with the justice building, which was completed a short time ago at a cost of $1,365,811. We have also a new post office being erected to conform with the general architectural beauty of that particular section of Ottawa, and costing $686,000. These may be classed as extravagant expenditures. All one has to do is to glance through the supplementary estimates, amounting to $122,000,000, which have been brought down, and pick out the public buildings and other works to be distributed throughout this country. At the same time let hon. members not overlook the proposed expenditures by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). They will find in those supplementary estimates a real pork-barrel for the next election. One can sympathize with the Minister of Finance in his effort to balance the budget against a drive of this kind on the federal treasury. We shall be told, no doubt, that these works are to cope with the great problem of unemployment. And this brings me to that problem.
I have listened for days, I was going to say for weeks, to debates on this problem, and I am more convinced than ever that if the Canadian people are given a chance they can solve this problem. I agree with the Minister of Finance that we must recreate in this country the spirit of cooperation and mutual helpfulness. The problem is a big one and must be attacked on a broad front. We have the machinery. Apart from governments we have the organization of industry, business and labour organizations, municipal bodies, church and welfare organizations, service clubs and many other bodies of citizens throughout the country; they extend to every city, town and hamlet; all are anxious to play their part to bring about better conditions. If we could only consolidate them; if each and all could be infused with a spirit of cooperation, what a mighty force we would have. We could then give effective battle to the foe which has invaded our country during the past few years. But to bring this about it would be necessary first to have strong leadership, and that leadership would have to come from the central or federal authority. Our federal government must give leadership. This government had a wonderful opportunity to give that leadership. They were returned to power with the largest following any government ever had. The provinces, with the exception of one or two, were of the same political faith. But this government failed. Not only did they fail to give leadership, but they adopted and followed a policy of shifting responsibility, shifting it to commissions, provinces, municipalites. That policy is responsible for our present condition and is going to make it a great deal more difficult to solve the problem to-day. I believe that every member of this house would regard it as ridiculous to suggest that unemployment can be taken care of, for all time, through government-provided work. What Canada must have is some revival of industry which will absorb great numbers of those who are now on our unemployment rolls. But industry must also be encouraged by means of a far-reaching Canadian fiscal policy.
I wish to deal briefly with one or two matters outside the budget. The first has to do with the question of settlement of European refugees in Canada. A short time ago the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) announced that a number of Sudeten Germans were to be brought to this country to be settled in British Columbia, and I understand that a number of them are to be placed on lands in the Fraser valley in what is known as the Pitt Meadows district.
I know there is considerable difference of opinion as to the bringing of these people to [DOT]this country and settling them in communities. It is not my intention to discuss at the present time that angle of the problem, but I do want to take this opportunity of registering a strong protest against placing these people on lands where they have no opportunity to make good. These lands in the Pitt Meadows district upon which these people are to be placed are unsuitable for settlement. I am told that during the last twenty years efforts have been made to settle the lands; they were at one time occupied by a large number of Mennonite families who were forced to abandon them because of consistent floods. I should like to quote what a resident has to say. This appeared in the Vancouver Province under date of March 24:
A resident of the Maple Ridge and Pitt Meadows districts for many years, John Dyke, writes to express his amazement at the proposal to place a number of German refugees on the bleak, desolate, water-sodden lands in the dyked areas of Pitt Meadows, north of the Alouette river. He says the lands are unsuitable for settlement, and the scheme is doomed to failure from the start.
"In spite of the costly dyking and pumping system the land is extremely difficult to drain. I would warn the authorities responsible if they do not wish to add to the number of relief recipients on their hands to find a more suitable area on which to place these people."
The Budget-Mr. Barber

I warn the government that if this settlement scheme is proceeded with, it will not only be disastrous to the settlers but mean that these people will drift into adjacent municipalities and become a charge on the country.
British Columbia being closer to the orient than is any other part of Canada we are naturally greatly concerned with what is taking place across the great Pacific. On behalf of a large number of decent people in that province I want to register a strong protest against the continuous export of scrap-iron and other munitions of war to Japan so that that country may carry on the mass murder of defenceless women and children of the great peace-loving nation of China. Surely we as Canadians do not want to play a part in this crime against humanity. The story of murder, barbarous cruelty, arson, banditry, and pillage that are involved in Japan's attempt to enslave the Chinese people is corroborated by foreign newspaper correspondents, writers, travellers, lecturers, educators and Christian missionaries. I have here a booklet that contains many of these reports from authenticated sources. It is entitled War in China; What it Means to Canada, by A. M. Stephen, and is issued by the China Aid Council and the National Salvation League of Vancouver. I quote from page 12:
Never, in the world's history, has the unleashed beast in man perpetrated horrors upon so vast a scale .as those going forward unchecked in China to-d.ay. Mr, Robert Norton, .the editor of the American magazine, "China To-day," is in possession of a documentary film that corroborates the stories of missionaries and correspondents and well-known and respected citizens of foreign concessions in China. Mr. Norton, in an article written under the caption, "Horror in Nanking," states: "From the moment that their troops entered, an indescribably terrible campaign of shooting, looting and rape began. They rounded up the population and searched the houses. Thousands were brought to the waterfront, where they were tied together in batches of fifty or more and done to death with machine guns, bayonets and in some oases with hand grenades. Gasoline was thrown over the bodies and they were set afire without too careful examination to determine whether all were dead. In a period of two months, 20,000 to 25,000 Chinese, according to estimates of foreigners in Nanking, were killed. No house was safe from looting. Thousands of women were seized and raped. Many were taken into the Japanese barracks and held there for weeks by the soldiers.
Why continue this ghastly record? This, my friends, is what the pro-Japanese apologists in Vancouver, B.C., term "war/' This is being done to innocent _ children in China by Canadian metals furnished by Canadian business men to the gangsters of Japan! Countless thousands of civilians, peaceful, friendly people, and innocent mothers and children are being slaughtered while we sit comfortably in our homes and listen to the voice that says, "Mind your own business!"

In 1937 we shipped, of metallic scrap, 35,536 tons, and in the same year we shipped, of iron and steel scrap, 68.309 tons. That is enough to mutilate thousands of women and children in China. I quote again:
The Dominion Bureau of Statistics shows that Canadian export of copper to Japan increased from $182,872 in 1934 to $1,300,473 in 1938; our export of nickel to Japan was $319,721 in 1934 as compared with $5,439,127 in 1938; our export of aluminum to Japan in 1937 was $1,947,847 and increased to $4,777,464 in 1938.
Will any sane person believe that any considerable portion of these metals are being used for the ordinary processes of peace?
I understand that under our Customs Act we have the power to control or to stop the shipment of war materials to aggressor nations. Surely it is not the desire of Canada to be a munitions dump for Japan. As one coming from British Columbia I urge that Canada lead in the application of an embargo on munitions to an aggressor nation. This is another opportunity for leadership on the part of this government.
I cannot conclude my remarks without expressing my concern over the state of agriculture to-day. In the district I have the honour to represent we have perhaps the finest dairy section in the country, but that industry is at a very low ebb to-day with milk prices down to a new low level-so low that it is almost impossible for farmers to carry on. Surpluses pile up with the problem of marketing the by-products manufactured from the surplus milk. I am of opinion that through the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce the government have failed to render the service that was expected of them in preventing the accumulation, and in the removal of surpluses from the Canadian market. The present proposal to purchase some 4,000,000 pounds of butter is not going to relieve the situation for the simple reason that this butter is not being removed from Canadian consumption. Bonusing is not a permanent remedy. We must adopt the orderly handling of exports of farm products, which would do more to stabilize prices. And that is another place where we want leadership from the federal government. I notice in the press that a committee representing eastern Canadian dairymen waited upon the government. From one of the local papers, dated April 15, I quote the following:
The committee members told cabinet minister that orderly handling of exports of farm products would, in their belief, have more influence on stabilization of prices prevailing for all products than any other measure. It would prevent price collapses and disastrously

The Budget-Mr. Jaques
low seasonal prices. Further, this policy would head off the need for emergency bonuses, and would be more permanently sound.
They also suggested a very small levy on the entire production of a certain product to provide a fund to re-imburse exporters who may incur a loss in their volume exported. Producers will stand the cost themselves rather than ask the government to take funds from the public treasury.
I urge the government to give serious consideration to the representations that have been made; and while the provinces are struggling with control legislation, let me urge that the government double its efforts to relieve the situation by removing these surpluses from the Canadian market.

I wish merely to read one or two resolutions that have been sent to me and to bring them to the notice of the house. The first one, which is from the Alberta Wool Growers' Association, reads:
Whereas, we view with alarm the rapidly growing threat to the Canadian woollen industry, brought about by the annually more exten-give practice on the part of manufacturers, ot deteriorating the quality of Canadian wools by mixing them with shoddy and other foreign materials, and selling the goods thus produced as Canadian woollen goods-this use of shoddy having increased from about 5,000,000 pounds in 1931 to 17,000,000 pounds in 1938,
And whereas this matter vitally affects the Canadian sheep raiser, and has an adverse effect on his revenue from his flock, through the reduced demand for virgin Canadian wool for the manufacture of fabric,
And whereas the reputation of Canadian wools suffers great injury by this destruction of their natural wearing qualities,
And whereas this matter is one of concern to every resident of Canada who purchases woollen goods for personal wear or household use, etc., as the deterioration of virgin wools by the admixture of shoddy makes more frequent replacements necessary, due to the shortened period of wear of these fabrics,
Be it therefore resolved that we ask the federal government of Canada to enact legislation, at this session of parliament, requiring all goods or fabrics made of wool, or of mixtures of wool, cotton, rayon, shoddy, or other materials, to bear a label stating the quantity or percentage of virgin wool, and of all other materials (including reworked wool) used in its manufacture (similar proposed legislation now being under consideration in the United States).
I should like to direct that to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) because as an old farmer I believe that in the end the raising of sheep will be the only solution to the problems of weeds and drifting soil; and any handicap to the raising of sheep in western Canada, or in Canada generally, should be removed. As I understand it, this resolution simply asks that the material bear a label stating the percentage of new or shoddy wool it contains.
The next resolution deals with a matter which was brought up by the last speaker, and comes from the Alberta section of the Canadian League for Peace:
We the undersigned petition the dominion government to place an embargo on war material from Canada to Japan.
I have not counted the signatures to this petition, but I believe there are close to one hundred, many of them the signatures of people well known to me.
The next resolution deals with immigration:
Whereas it is understood that _the_ federal government is contemplating shipping in many thousands of immigrants for settlement in western Canada, and .	.	.
Whereas any .additional competition in the producing of farm products will have a depressing effect on a market now staggering under a heavy load of so-called overproduction, Therefore be it resolved that this group go on record as being bitterly opposed to the dumping in our midst of any more immigrants as long as the ruinous present prices for farm products exist, and
Be it further resolved that a copy of this resolution be sent to our provincial government and a copy to the Prime Minister, Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King.
That is from the Wetaskiwin constituency association of the Alberta Social Credit League.
The next resolution is one which was recently passed by the legislature of Manitoba. It was introduced by Miss Salome Halldorson, Social Credit member for the constituency of St. George, Manitoba. It reads:
Whereas Canada is -a sovereign nation with a democratic constitution;
Whereas in a sovereign democracy the people are the supreme authority to determine the results which shall accrue to them from the administration of their affairs;
Whereas the abundant resources of the nation and ithe national capacity to produce render it physically possible to give economic security and freedom to every citizen-results which the sovereign people of the dominion desire;
And whereas the present condition of poverty, indigence, insecurity and economic impotence constitute a denial of the sovereignty of the people;
Be it resolved by this democratic legislature of the province of Manitoba which is entrusted with the welfare of the people of this province, that we do hereby urge that the parliament of Canada ensure to our people their democratic rights by instructing the appropriate institutions and in particular the banking institutions, to forthwith order their methods of administration in such a way as to give the people of the nation the conditions .and results that they desire and that they know to be physically possible.
That resolution was passed by a vote of twenty-eight, to nineteen. Among those voting for the resolution were thirteen Liberals, six
Conservatives, five Social Crediters and four independents.

subtopic: DEDATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has improved in health. I am sorry that in his recovery, however, he did not recapture some of those healthy Liberal principles with which he was imbued when he first came out of the west. I wish this budget had been more robust. It is a far cry from that May day budget which was based upon those fundamental principles that the Minister of Finance learned in his long association with the humble farmers on the western plains. Those were the days when he believed in Liberal principles, before he became enamoured of the doctrine of the inevitability of gradualness.
This budget has been called by the press of Canada a business man's budget. It certainly is not a poor man's budget. This year's financial statement of the country differs but little from its predecessor in regard to providing any hope for those who have suffered from depressions and recessions. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the budget places me in a position similar to that of the employee who was to be discharged and who said that if he was to be discharged he was glad that it would be done politely. There is slight consolation in being discharged at any time, and the consolation I can find in this budget or this financial statement is indeed slight. In fact,
I think it is a deliberate betrayal of the western electorate. And in order that this house may know that my tariff views are not just a brain wave on my part, I am going to quote from the comment appearing in the Winnipeg Free Press of April 26 in regard to this budget:
There will be undisguised disappointment in western Canada that, faced with the urgent need of increasing his sources of revenue, the finance minister refused to do the obvious thing and slash at the general structure of tariff in order to fulfil a twin purpose: (1) to reduce consumers' costs and (2) to make it more of a tariff for revenue and less of a protective, prohibitory tariff. . . . But some day it will become very clear to Hr. Dunning and his colleagues that, by leaving the tariff at its present level, they have betrayed one of the strongest hopes which this country (and particularly the west) held for them when they came to power in 1935.

I wish to bring before the house two authorities on this tariff structure, and I want the house to know that I am not just one of those tariff thumpers from western Canada, as a certain Textile Journal stated with regard to the western low tariff members. I want to point out that in western Canada tariffs are our natural enemies. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) prepared a brief for Nova Scotia in 1931. In that brief I find he states:
A tariff policy with a true national objective would recognize the importance of maintaining the health of industries, dependent upon export markets, especially as such industries are essential to the [DOT]economic development of seven of the nine provinces of the dominion. In recognition of this fact these industries, agriculture, mining, fishing and lumbering would be relieved at least of tariff duties on all instruments of production essential to their operation. In other words the vital interest of seven provinces in lower costs of production in primary industries compelled to sell their products in world markets would be given priority over considerations urged in support of the manufacture of these instruments of production in Canada behind a protective tariff.
Let me quote from the figures as they are set out by the Minister of Labour in that 'brief, when he points out what the west pays in tariff. These are the figures:
Manitoba	$29,185,740
Saskatchewan	 29,228,285
Alberta	  27,909,396
Total	$86,323,421
In the conclusions which he sums up in his brief the minister says:
Upon these various premises, it is urged that Nova Scotia is entitled to relief and compensation, not merely in pursuance of the assurances given on the occasion of its entrance into the Canadian federation, but also on the broad equitable ground that the federation defeats its primary purpose if through its constitutional arrangements or through policies instituted by the national government it accomplishes a gradual debilitation of one or more of the provincial communities of which it is composed.
Some may say that was back in 1931; that was in the days when the present minister was professor of economics and political science in Queen's university. Others have stated that his figures were high, and that perhaps times were better then than they are to-day. But what has Doctor Jacob Viner, a noted authority on tariffs, to say? He made an intensive study for Manitoba, in his first presentation of November, 1938. His observations were presented to the interprovincial relations commission. In his first presentation he placed the average tariff burden on the prairies at $58,000,000. Subsequently, on account of abjection to various items raised, Doctor Viner revised his estimates with

The Budget-Mr. Fleming
extreme care, making adjustments, some downward and some upward, with the net result that he finds the average annual tariff burden in normal years on the prairies is $47,000,000. This is what he says at page 40 of his brief before the royal commission:
From our original estimate of $58,000,000 as the tariff burden in a year of normal expenditures of the people of the prairie provinces we have subtracted approximately $33,000,000 in correction of errors in our favour. We have replaced $20,000,000 of this deduction because of deliberate omissions from our original estimate to take care of possible errors in our favour, and $2,000,000 has been added to our estimate to provide for tariff burden in connection with purchases at wholesale. We therefore obtain, after making all corrections for which we can find reasonable basis, $47,000,000 as our final estimate of .the added cost to the people of the prairie provinces in a year of normal expenditures, resulting from the price enhancement brought -about by the Canadian protective tariff.
Mr. Speaker, I think after we see those two viewpoints expressed, it would only be fair if we took a point between them. It is no wonder that last year, when speaking in this House of Commons, the Minister of Labour said that we in western Canada were entitled to compensating adjustments. If we were not given a promise last year and the year before and the year before that, certainly the hope was held up to us by the present government that if the west did not get concessions indirectly through the United States trade treaties, we would get them directly through the budget. Every year I have protested about the high price of farm implements. and I produced evidence to show that there was a combine working as an effective monopoly in the manufacture of farm implements. I lamented this to the government, but they did nothing about it. Once again I lament, and once again I deplore it and say that something must be done or the Liberal party in Canada will regret it.
The other night the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Johnston), when speaking in the House of Commons, was apologetic about asking for SO cents as a minimum price for wheat. He took what I would term a defeatist viewpoint, stating that we were only eleven per cent of the voting power of this house. Be that as it may, I will say here that I will continue my fight for an 80 cent minimum price for wheat, and an acreage bonus as well. The hon. member for Lake Centre reminds me very much of a character that one sees every day in the newspapers. He is bold and defiant and has plenty of reckless courage while associating with western farmers, but in the presence of the ministry he abandons those principles with the most surprising ease. In fact, his courage disappears
like the mist before the rising sun. He seems to be more or less ashamed to ask for 80 cents as a minimum price for wheat.
In answer to my question about the tariff receipts that we pour into Canada, he said I should hold my soul in patience. But, Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to do this when we see the farmers of Saskatchewan fast becoming economic serfs, when we see children suffering from malnutrition, when we see families of eight and ten living on $8 a month-and then when we see government counsel getting $200 a day, and when we see some of our superior court judges drawing down $9,000 a year who, because they do a little work for the federal government, receive $35 a day as living allowance.
Is it any wonder the western wheat farmer is becoming suspicious? I regret government aid; the farmer does not want charity, but what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander since we have contributed $50,000,000 a year to our national economy-not to-day, but since we came into confederation, by the autonomy bills of 1905. The industrial east will readily tell us that no industry can exist for long if production costs constantly exceed selling prices.
Wheat has also a fixed cost of production, more so than any other industry, because other types of industry can more readily reduce labour costs. The farmer does not get a salary, unless there is profitable operation. And, Mr. Speaker, eliminate the farmer and what have you left? Surely no one contends that we should eliminate the great wheat industry of western Canada? Nor do I believe that many persons contend that this depressed condition for the western wheat farmer is permanent. We are facing an emergency condition and it should be met with emergency measures. We are not demanding bonuses; we are simply asking for a compensating adjustment. The east has demanded protection for years. It is only fair that the west should have some assistance when she needs it, and when it is necessary for the welfare of our whole Canadian economy. Tariffs protect the margin of profit. Wheat assistance lowers the margin of loss. If the government sets the price of wheat at 80 cents we give an injection into the heart of this Canadian economy of ours, and the blood will go coursing through its body again, giving new life and new hope. But if we let that heart die, then surely we will die. The whole economic structure of western Canada has been built up and capitalized on the predication of a certain revenue from wheat. But to guarantee a price that is below subsistence level is not
The Budget-Mr. Fleming

assistance; it leads the east to the belief that something is being done for the west, and it tries to create the impression in the west that the government is assuming somewhat of its obligation to the western wheat farmer. The Minister of Finance, as reported at page 3142 of Hansard-[DOT]

speechtext:
I was just about to quote from the budget speech of the Minister of Finance. I consider that is in order. My remarks up to that time were based upon the radio address by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and I had no thought in mind of commenting on any bill now before the house. The Minister of Finance said this:
Agriculture can do little to protect itself against these international storms. Other producers can contract their output, can frequently lay off their workers to live at public cost upon the relief rolls, while their contraction in output prevents a disastrous decline in price and the disappearance of profits. Farmers cannot readily do these things.

And again:
This was the reason for the guarantee of a basic minimum price of 80 cents for the western wheat crop of last year.
The minister states that this was the reason for a guarantee of a basic minimum price of 80 cents, but he does not say anything about the 60 cent price the Minister of Agriculture mentioned in his address over the radio in Saskatchewan during the Easter recess. If there were justification for the 80 cent price last year, there is just as much, if not more, for it this year.

subtopic: DEDATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not mention a 60 cent price in my radio address.

subtopic: DEDATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister said a 60 cent advance.

subtopic: DEDATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not a 60 cent price.

subtopic: DEDATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is splitting hairs,
and I think I told the minister that before. The livelihood of the whole prairie west depends upon the industry of agriculture. The whole economy that has been built up is threatened with extinction by this 60 cent price. The farmer cannot live on 60 cent wheat. All the figures having to do with industry prove that is below the cost of production. The farmers of the west have been aroused by what they regard as a betrayal of their interests. We western members might just as well bluntly tell the government right now what we think of the matter. I protest that the farmers of the west cannot be satisfied with anything less than 80 cents. Whether or not there is a 60 cent advance, that is the lowest basic price upon which we can exist and have something with which to pay on our debts. The price of wheat this year, according to the bureau of statistics, is the lowest since 1890, with the exception of 1932. Government assistance is needed when the price of wheat is low, not when it is high. Surely no Liberal member of parliament would rise in his place in this house and say that he would be willing to let 300.000 people in western Canada starve. I am getting sick and disgusted hearing all about the relief that has been poured into the west, just as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) said he was getting sick and tired talking about tariffs. Other places than western Canada get relief.
I sometimes wonder if the reason why we are not seeking markets is that we do not wish to sell wheat to potential enemies. England knows where her wheat supply is in the event of war. While I am not questioning that as a matter of policy, I do not see why the wheat farmer should have to suffer.

The Budget-Mr. Fleming
It is not that we want to be war-threat profiteers. On the contrary, it looks as though we are going to be war-threat victims. We all remember the story of what happened in 1917 when the price of wheat soared to $2.50 a bushel. There was great consternation in the financial world of St. James street, Montreal, and Bay street, Toronto. They considered that this was an exorbitant price, and they prevailed upon the government of the day to set a price on wheat. They were afraid the agricultural west might become a financial factor, and a stop price was placed on this commodity. They might have received $5 a bushel, but the tillers of the soil, the back-bone of Canada, were not to be allowed to get into that class. That strata of society was just for the manufacturer of the east. It was quite in order for the textile industry, the packing houses and the drug supply houses to make this money; that was quite justifiable ; but the humble peasants in the lowly cottages from the head of the lakes to the Rocky mountains must not make too much profit, that would be disloyalty to their king and country.
The Minister of Finance says;
On the frontiers of science, invention and technology, the possibilities of expansion are greater than they ever were on the geographical frontier.
Perhaps he had in mind how they are making buttons out of skim-milk in Waterloo county. But while these frontiers of technology have been expanding, apparently our ability to control them has been contracting. Thus not only do I see little hope for the west in the budget, but I fail to find any minor, let alone any major attempt to tackle the great economic problems of the day. Many persons believe that the invidious paradox of poverty amidst plenty and our economic failure are due entirely to our outworn monetary system.
I turn now to another subject. The minister said that naked aggression has caused a grim procession of tragedies and repeatedly altered the map of Europe. This has had its effect in Canada although we are far removed from the conflict of war in Europe. I often wonder if the Canadian people fully realize how fortunate they are in having as Prime Minister, the right hon. leader of the Liberal party (Mr. Mackenzie King). One thing for which we must be thankful is his effort to keep us out of war. The influence that Canada has in restraining the old land from any hasty action may never be fully known, and I shiver to think what might have happened if a hot-head had been at the head of our administration.
Imperialism and flag-waving are with us once again. Hon. members must see it on every side with its propaganda of fear. This proved a suitable way of getting into parliament in 1917, and no one knows it better than the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Johnston), and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion). The unscrupulous office seekers are at work again trying to cast reflection upon our German and Ukrainian population. History repeats itself; the same old tactics that were used in 1917 are again to be seen. Even the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Woodsworth) raised a question the other day in the house about a certain German newspaper in Winnipeg. I never heard the hon. gentleman raise any question about communistic propaganda. He was loud in his condemnation of padlock law in the old province of Quebec when it attempted to stamp out communism.

speechtext:
Are you in favour
of it?

subtopic: DEDATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, if it stamps out
communism. Communism is not a social and political system, but a gigantic conspiracy organized throughout the world to wage war against all human and divine laws and to destroy Christian civilization, according to the Cardinal Archbishop of Quebec. Our German population is now being subjected to violent abuse. For a quarter of a century I have lived in a German speaking community, and I number members of that community among my truest and best friends. It is indeed with sorrow in my heart that I hear them subjected to insult. The German-Canadian citizens of Saskatchewan are loyal to their king and country, and loyal to Canadian institutions. There may be some irresponsible agitators who are trying to embarrass our German population, just as some of our English-speaking people try to embarrass us. I think I can best give to the house an idea of the loyalty of our German-Canadians of Saskatchewan by quoting from a German language newspaper published in the city of Regina, a paper that has been published for over thirty years. In one of its leading editorials Der Courier says:
The majority of German-Canadians now in this country are pro-British with unmistakable loyalty to the land of their adoption.
Der Courier has in the past denounced communism as a disrupting, demoralizing influence in our Canadian life. It does not hesitate to denounce any other similar fact that such a disturbing organization finds advocates among a few German-speaking citizens makes no difference to the principle involved. Der Courier stands for national unity, freedom of speech, liberty of action and democratic government. It is resolutely opposed to any movement
The Budget*-Mr. Fleming

which would undermine or imperil these privileges which Canadians enjoy in such generous measure.
Throughout the long years of its existence Der Courier has interested itself in the democratic and political life of Canada. It has steadfastly striven to discharge, even at the price of sacrifice, its duty in directing public opinion along sane paths. It has endeavoured to promote peace and harmony among all peoples, races and creeds. It has held high and exalted concept of citizenship and has emphasized the liberties, privileges and duties which that citizenship entails. It has always endeavoured to be impartial, temperate and cool in judgment, free from racial or religious bias. In a word, it has tried to be constructive, not destructive, in character. Its aim has been to build, not to destroy.
I have a letter from a young Ukrainian in my constituency, in which he says:
As to the Ukrainians here in Canada, they are loyal to the British empire and willing to fight against the British enemy that will try to disturb her peace and our freedom. .	.	.
All Ukrainians will fight shoulder to shoulder with the British army against any enemy who would try to disturb our peace and freedom.
Our non-British population have confidence in the present Prime Minister. They recall 1917, when the government of Canada brought into existence the nefarious War-time Elections Act, which disfranchised them and made a sham of our Canadian franchise. While we must be alive to defend ourselves if attacked, that is a far cry from inciting people to hate, which is neither Christian nor the way to peace. Let me recall to this house the words of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier who, speaking on this disfranchising bill, said:
Because they may have been born in Germany or Austria or Turkey they are not sup-posed_ to give an unbiased verdict upon the questions before the country. I do not admit that doctrine. I do not admit the doctrine that when a man leaves Europe-whatever may be the part of Europe whence he comes-and comes to this country, when he swears allegiance to His Majesty the King, when he becomes a citizen of Canada, when he builds a home for himself and his family, I am not prepared to believe that if a conflict arises between the land of that man's birth and the land of his adoption, that he will go back upon the country to which he has sworn allegiance. I can well believe that if there be men of German origin who have forsaken Germany and who have become British subjects in this country-having made their homes here and established their families here-that they may be suffering agony at this time, but I am not prepared to believe that they will turn traitor to the land of their adoption in favour of the land of their birth.
That can well be repeated to-day not only for the truth of what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said, but also as a warning to those who might be thinking of following people who would use
[Mr. Fleming.1
the cheap trick of appealing to patriotism and race prejudice in order to gain political preferment.
I find, Mr. Speaker, that this budget in no way provides help for our suffering population. There is no help for the primary producer; nothing has been done with respect to farm implements; nothing has been done to smash the combines about which we heard so much a year ago. The sales tax has not been abolished. The sugar tax is still maintained. I therefore find that I must support the amendment to the amendment. I do so because I believe it is in the interests of the people whom I represent in this house, and because I wish to register with this government my protest. I wish, however, to make it abundantly clear to the house and the country that I cannot subscribe to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation doctrine of socialism. Perhaps I can explain my views more forcefully by quoting the words of a distinguished Canadian, Cardinal Villeneuve, who, speaking in Montreal last fall, said:
Now I will deal with my attitude towards the C.C.F. One of the principal leaders of the C.C.F. declared that their program was based on frankly socialist principles. That is true; the C.C.F. and communism, economic programs are practically the same. The only difference is that the communists admit that they are prepared to attain their object by violent means, while the C.C.F. think they will accomplish their purpose peacefully.
The C.C.F. program contains several fundamental errors. Let me very briefly describe the first error in the C.C.F. program which advocates the suppression or at least the quasisuppression of private property. Now the right to own property is not derived from human laws but from nature, and every man has by nature the right to possess property as his own.
The abolition of private ownership leads to state ownership and therefore the C.C.F. program proposes the nationalization of practically all forms of industry and other means of production and state ownership of all financial companies, etc.
I cannot support the Tory amendment because it is worse even than the budget. Since I have come to this house I have found five types of Tories. There is, first, the Toronto Tory, represented by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). As one Conservative said, " If in doubt, vote as the member for Broadview does and you will always get Tory votes in Toronto."
Next there are the sincere Tories, represented by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence), a bom high-protectionist, and always consistent.
Then there are the insincere Tories, represented by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley)-a Tory in Toronto and a Cooperative Commonwealth Federationist in Assiniboia.

The Budget-Mr. Fleming

subtopic: DEDATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What kind of a Liberal is the hon. member?

subtopic: DEDATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am a western low-tariff Liberal.
Next there are the Liberal Tories, represented by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), a convert to Toryism, and converts are always much more ardent in their new faith than if natural born to it.
Finally there are the Tory Liberals. I shall not give examples for fear Israel Tarte might haunt them in their sleep and say to them, " Laurier kicked me out of the Liberal administration because I was a high-protectionist, but I was much more moderate than you are."
I have found, Mr. Speaker, in the last few months, that these various types of Toryism look upon the west as a millstone round their necks. We in the west are to them a sort of Albanian colony in this confederation which Macdonald made and Laurier saved. If this cleavage is allowed to grow, I fear that great northern nation which was the dream of D'Arcy McGee will become " warring nations in the bosom of a single state." Do not let us say that the credit of Canada cannot pay an assessment for a minimum price for wheat. The governor of the Bank of Canada admitted, under cross-examination by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), that we could spend billions of dollars and in no way impoverish this country. I should like to quote at this point from a speech by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard who, speaking at St. Thomas on April 22, is reported as follows:
The speaker told of other things that "bankrupt" Germany had done. The hundreds of costly public buildings, the great new sports and health stadium, a new university at Munich that Hitler had ordered built when the need of a new wing to the old university was voiced. "It is true they have regimentation of wealth and manpower in Germany, that they work longer hours at lower wages, but that has nothing to do with the fact that Germany could find the equivalent of 4,000 million gold dollars to build all this," said the speaker. "The ability of finding money, as exampled in the totalitarian nations, should give the answer to that silly question often heard propounded in Canada: 'Where is the money coming from'."
We have the best land in the world. Our resources are unsurpassed in the world. What *would Hitler not give for those fertile wheat fields? But, Mr. Speaker, the agrarian west will not much longer live in economic slavery. The farmer sells for nothing the fruit of his toil, but when he purchases he has to pay out of all proportion to his income. Let the government be magnanimous; let them give the western farmer an 80 cent minimum price and the acreage bonus as well. I hope that
this government will not become what Disraeli once said about the Conservative party. "A Conservative government is an organized hypocrisy."
In the last few weeks the Winnipeg Free Press has been publishing cartoons, with a certain degree of humour, by Arch Dale, the official cartoonist of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. On one side there is a figure represented by the Bracken committee; on the other, a member of the present government, and then, between the two, a hard-pressed farmer. Dale brought home to us the other day the bitter fight which the farmers and farm leaders of western Canada are putting up, and he quoted that phrase from Emerson which we learned years ago in our public school readers:
By the rude bridge that arched the flood.
Their flag to April's breeze unfurled,
Here once the embattled farmers stood.
And fired the shot heard round the world.
The shot for economic liberty has been fired. Let the Liberal government take cognizance of these democratic petitions which were presented to the government by the Bracken committee. Someone has said that committee came down here and held a pistol to the head of the government. That is far from the truth. The petition is one of the weapons which the farmers of western Canada has, in our democratic set-up, to show what they are thinking about on the western plains.
Let me say in conclusion that I regret the necessity of offering any opposition to the government's budget, but I do so because I learned at my mother's knee to be true to yourself and to no man will you be false. I recall that on the day I received the Liberal nomination in the constituency of Humboldt I quoted the words of that great Liberal, William Lyon Mackenzie, grandfather of the leader of the present government:
I have no end in view save the well-being
of the people at large, no ambition to serve buit thiat of contributing to the happiness and the prosperity of our common country. The influence and the authority "with which you may invest me, shall always be directed according to the best of my judgment, for the general good, and it will be my care to uphold your right to the utmost of my power with the firmness, moderation and perseverance, which becomes the representative of a free people.
Yet if year after year we are to have a series of innocuous budgets, such as this is, I am almost willing to try any change. I just want to give this warning to the government: If this budget indicates the answer to our problems, particularly to the sorely pressed west, then I despair of the future for the Liberal party in western Canada.
The Budget-Mr. Marshall

subtopic: DEDATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Fleming) upon delivering a constructive speech. To my mind he usually makes a forward contribution to the debates of this house. It takes courage for any supporter of a government to rise in his place and speak his mind as the hon. member has done this evening.
I wish to give a moment or two to a remark which was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Tomlinson). He made a brief reference to the group of which I am a member to the effect that we social crediters dislike the eastern people because they have but one desire, namely, to grab all they can lay their hands on. Let me hasten to state that this is not the truth. Centred in eastern Canada to-day are financial institutions which have brought the people of western Canada to the poverty-stricken condition in which they find themselves to-day, and they have also brought to the same condition a very large percentage of the people of eastern Canada. We are opposed to these institutions on account of their nefarious practices, not because of what they have done to western Canadians but because of what they have done to all the people of Canada, both in the east and in the west. We were sent here by people who have come to realize what is the cause of their troubles. These people know that debt, taxation and the low price of farm products are the causes of the situation in which they find themselves. They know full well that these debt merchants and manipulators of the prices of primary products live in eastern Canada, and our people are determined through their elected representatives to see that an end is made of this unholy traffic; that is the reason we are here to-day.
We have no quarrel with eastern Canadians. The west was peopled by men and women who came from eastern Canada or who can trace their lineage back to families that lived in Ontario, Quebec, or even the maritime provinces. Everything that the hon. member for Bruce can persuade this government to do for eastern Canada will find ready support so far as we are concerned, provided, of course, that his requests are fair, just and ' reasonable, because we are opposed to anything which smacks of graft or political patronage.
If we are to judge from the speech delivered by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Hynd-man), this afternoon, there is something wrong in eastern Canada. It appears that patronage is rampant even in the city in which we are holding this parliament. We as a group want for all our citizens, whether they
rMr. Fleming.]
live in the east or the wrest, justice, equity, the right to live normal, happy, contented lives, free from debt and worry. We are deeply concerned with the plight of the fishermen of Nova Scotia or of British Columbia; we are deeply concerned over the problems of the apple growers of the Annapolis valley or of the Okanagan. We share their worries with the cheesemakers and the potato growers of Ontario. Their problems are our concern just as much as are the problems of the people of the prairies. I say this to the Liberal party to-night: You will find us as a group ready and willing to sit round a common table at any time with only one object in mind, namely, a sincere desire to find a solution to the problem of debt, which, to my mind, transcends every other problem under the sun.
When I hear so many hon. members quoting statements made in past days by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), or the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), or the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), or even the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), there comes to my recollection time and time again a statement made by the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) which, in my opinion, far exceeds anything I have ever heard from the point of view of optimism. I brought this statement to the attention of the house in the first session of the present parliament in 1936, and I make no apology for quoting it again on this occasion. In fact, it is a statement which we should constantly keep fresh in our memories. Here it is. The Minister of Mines and Resources made a broadcast to the Canadian people on the evening of April 24, 1936, at 10.30 o'clock eastern standard time, and at the conclusion of his broadcast he made this astonishing statement:
Is it .too much to expect that production of gold in Canada of from $200,000,000 to $250,000,000 -a year would give the following results:
1.	Decisively and permanently settle the problem of unemployment.
2.	Bridge the gap between the east and the west with mining camps and communities established at numerous points.
3.	Bring a constructive and probably a permanent solution ,to our railroad problem.
4.	Create an even greater market than at present for foodstuffs, clothing, structural materials, mine machinery and equipment, electrical supplies, electric power, fuel, explosives and innumerable other commodities including household furnishings and automobiles.
5.	Revitalize the whole national economic life of the dominion.
6.	Open up careers for coming generations of university graduates.
7.	Ease the financial problems of the dominion, provinces and municipalities.

The Budget-Mr. Marshall
8.	Alleviate the burden of our international indebtedness.
9.	Assure the stability of the Canadian dollar; and. finally,
10.	Stimulate the opening up and development of our resources in those northlands about which we know little to-day.
We must not fail to grasp t)he opportunity that lies before us.
If we turn to the white paper that formed a part of the budget this year, we shall find on page 27 that the production of gold has advanced steadily from 1926 to the present time. The production has been as follows:
1926	$ 36,300,000
1928	 39,100,000
1932	 71,500,000
1936		 131.300,000
1937		 143,300,000
1938		 165,900,000
We are steadily aproaching the $200,000,000 mark. But will anyone suggest that unemployment is gradually decreasing as the production of gold is increasing? Will anyone suggest that poverty is declining in the same ratio as gold is increasing? I think that statement by the Minister of Mines and Resources is one of the most extravagant utterances ever made, unless I do not realize what the meaning of the word " extravagant " actually is. Some of the statements that the Prime Minister has made pale into insignificance compared with this statement.
This budget that we are considering at the present time is the fourth in the new series of Liberal budgets presented to the people of Canada for their acceptance or condemnation according to the way in which the people look upon them. This is the ninth successive year in which a deficit has been registered. These deficits have ranged from $220,000,000 in 1933 to a little more than $17,000,000 in 1937-38.
I always admire the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman), and I listen to him with great interest when he speaks. He interjects into his speeches little quips and sallies that create at times pleasant diversion. A couple of years ago this hon. gentleman used a couplet that had its birth in the house of representatives of the United States. He dressed it up in slightly different clothes and applied it to the present premier of Alberta, and the house got quite a nice laugh out of it. I want to bring it to the attention of the house in its original form. It is this:
Hush, little deficit, don't you cry;
You'll be a crisis by and by.
I believe right thinking people in Canada to-day will agree that the crisis is not in the sweet by and by; it is here to-day. It is a tragedy to think that the intelligence displayed
by the members of the Liberal party in this house has not been able to bring about a solution of the problems which confront us.
While on the subject of debt and deficits I should like to refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood) on April 14, appearing at page 2801 of Hansard:
We have enjoyed sane, economic administration. If one were to check the debt of Canada as it stands to-day, if he were to add all the surpluses under Liberal administrations and those under Conservative administrations, and balance them against the deficits of these respective parties, he would find that only $23,000,000 of a total interest-bearing debt of $3,100,000,000 can be attributed to Liberal administration.
A little further on he said, referring to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey):
How can the hon. member be sincere in his eloquence for the youth of Canada when the party to which he belongs has been guilty of saddling youth with more debt and has done more to mortgage future generations than any other party in Canada.
I took the trouble to do just as he suggested, and if any hon. member wishes to check the figures I am about to give he will find them at page 60 of the public accounts for 1938. The Liberals have been in office thirty-two years. During twenty-one years they piled up deficits and during eleven years they showed surpluses. They increased the public debt by $505,624,853.13, and during the eleven years they showed surpluses they decreased the public debt by $291,125,038.55. The difference between these two figures, or $214,499,814.58, is the net amount that has been added to the debt of this country by the Liberal party. That is a far cry from the S23.000,000 mentioned in the speech of the hon. member. But I wish to go on and complete the picture. The Conservatives have been in office thirty-five years, during thirty-one of which they showed deficits, while in the remaining four they had surpluses. They increased the national debt by SI.377,724,209.18. while they decreased the national debt by $27,977,780.77. The difference between these two figures, or $1,349,746,428.41, is the amount by which the national debt has been increased by the Conservative party since confederation. Then, during four years we had a union government, a fusion of the Liberal and Conservative parties.

speechtext: No; it was all Tory.

speechtext:
I am glad to hear that statement. I did not know; I thought it was composed of both parties. During those four years the national debt was increased by $1,461,692,685.89. I wonder whether the Liberals or the Conservatives will derive much
The Budget-Mr. Marshall

consolation from those figures. I suggest that at the next election, whether it is held this year or next, the Canadian people will judge both the Liberals and the Conservatives on their past records. The creation of debt instead of the creation of currency and credit will be the national issue in the next election, unless I am greatly mistaken.
On page 3147 of Hansard of this year the Minister of Finance said:
Our taxes are high but w-e do not bury the money we take in in taxes, as one might gather from what some speakers say. We spend it quickly, far too quickly, in my opinion, and for the most part pass it on to those who will spend it quickly again.
Perhaps hon. members might be interested to learn where we get our tax dollars and how we spend them. During the year just ended the income tax accounted for 28-31 cents in every tax dollar. The sales tax accounted for 23-81 cents; customs for 15-70 cents; excise for 10-23 cents, and other sources for 21-95 cents. The point I wish to make here is that one year ago the greatest money-getter of all was the sales tax. This year it has fallen to second place and its former position has been taken temporarily by the income tax. The sales tax, which is 8 per cent on the manufacturer's invoice, is one of the greatest impositions that could be placed upon the backs of the people. When it reaches the consumer, instead of its being 8 per cent it amounts to, roughly speaking, 12 per cent. An interesting item in connection with these matters is that the people of the institutions which make the most out of the people of Canada pay the least. On page 2 of the white paper we find that taxes collected from banking institutions have steadily decreased from 1934-35 to the present time. These are the figures of the amounts collected from these institutions:
